5. Mr Habibul Islam Bhuiyan, learned Advocate with Mr Syed Mokaddas Ali, learned Advocate appearing for the complainant opposite party, on the other hand, submits that if we read the complaint minutely then we find it disclose sufficient ingredients of section 138 of the Negotiable Instruments and, as such, the proceeding should not be quashed. Mr Habibul Islam Bhuiyan, learned Advocate, referred to the decisions of Munshi Md Rashed Kamal vs Abdus Salam reported in 10 BLC (AD) 186 and Habibur Rahman Howlader vs State reported in 53 DLR (AD) 111. We will discuss these decisions later on. 

 7. On a reading of these two sub-sections of section 138 of the Act it appears that after presenting the cheque in bank, if the cheque is dishonoured, thereafter, after 15 days of the receipt of the information, the legal notice is to be served. Let us see whether the complainant fulfilled the required conditions of law. Paragraph 3 of the complaint speaks that the complainant presented "above mentioned four cheques" through its account. We do not find from this statement the date of presentation of the cheques. Again from this paragraph we see "But the said Basic Bank Limited on several occasions returned all the cheques without making payment due to insufficiency of fund in the account." Here we also do not find any specific date when the complainant received the information. We also find four cheques were presented to the complainant by the accused petitioner and four cheques are of different dates. A cheque may be presented, as held by the Appellate Division of the Hon'ble Supreme Court in the decision reported in 10 BLC, as many times the complainant desires but that must be within six months. But in the given case we find that there is no specific date as to when the cheques were presented and when the complainant received the information. This is a legal bar for initiating a proceeding under section 138 of the Negotiable Instruments Act. Moreso, we find from paragraph No. 4 that notices were sent twice, one on 27-10-2004 and another on 3rd November, 2004. Law permits presenting of the cheque for as many times as the complainant desires, but the notice should be served only for once as per law, repeated notices cannot be served as subsequent issuance of notices are nothing but a clever device to overcome the limitation prescribed under clauses 1(b) and (c) of section 138 of the Act. It appears that first notice was issued on 27-10-2004 and next was on 3-11-2004. Instant proceeding was initiated on 25-11-2004, long after the period mentioned in, 138(C) of the Act. The decisions reported in 10 BLC, 9 BLC and 53 DLR, the cases mentioned in those decisions are not like the complaint of the instant case. In the petition of complaint of the instant case, it does not disclose the date of the presentation of the cheques nor disclose when the complainant received the information from the Bank and moreso, in the instant case, repeated notices were issued which is not permissible under section 138 of the Act. Furthermore, as we find, that, after issuing of notice on 27-10-2004 and 3-11-2004, there is no date mentioned as to whether the accused petitioner received those notices or not. We also find that from 27-10-2004 i.e. when the 1st notice was issued, the instant case was filed on 25-11-2004, which is also beyond the period mentioned under section 138(1)(C) of the Act. Moreover, it appears that against 4 dishonored cheques the accused petitioner made a single complaint which is also not permissible under law. Law speaks one cheque will give rise to one case. Another aspect of the case that whatever was done in the instant case was done by the accused petitioner as proprietor of the Regent Auto under an agreement in between two companies, but Regent Auto has not been made a party in the proceeding.
